claude.sample_unit: gastroenterologists (6 AI-assisted, 6 unassisted) reading static endocytoscopy images
models_evaluated: ResNet-based CNN ensemble (5 models, fivefold cross-validation)

links.outcome: Gastroenterologist sensitivity and accuracy with versus without AI assistance at follow-up; overreliance assessed
links.effect: AI-assisted gastroenterologists had higher sensitivity (+20.0%, p=0.025) and accuracy (+12.22%, p=0.050) than unassisted ones at follow-up; untrained users showed reduced reliance on AI after training.
links.quote: When tested at 23.3 (±9.1) days after training, AI-assisted gastroenterologists maintained higher sensitivity (+20.0% (3.14–36.86), p = 0.025) and accuracy (+12.22% (0.03–24.48), p = 0.050) for recognizing dysplasia than the unassisted gastroenterologists.

links.outcome: Clinician diagnostic performance with AI support versus without, compared with AI alone
links.effect: After cross-over, gastroenterologists with AI exceeded their own sensitivity (+24.45%, p=0.020) and accuracy (+13.33%, p=0.039) and outperformed the AI model alone on sensitivity (+12.89%, p=0.024).
links.quote: Additionally, they outperformed the sensitivity of the AI model alone (+12.89% (2.11–23.67), p = 0.024) ( Figure 4 D).

links.outcome: Whether users detect incorrect AI outputs / overreliance before and after training
links.effect: Trained gastroenterologists made fewer false negatives on AI-correct images (6.7% vs 37.5%, p=0.038); rejection of correct AI positives 3.8% vs 7.9% (p=0.325); AI calls fell from 90% to 57.8% after training.
links.quote: Notably, the trained gastroenterologists made fewer false negative diagnoses in images that otherwise would have been correctly predicted by AI (6.7% (3/45) vs. 37.5% (3/8), p = 0.038).

links.outcome: Effect of training on reliance on AI and diagnostic performance
links.effect: Untrained gastroenterologists with AI access called for AI in 90% of cases before training, dropping to 57.8% after training (p<0.001) and 75.6% at follow-up; trained users better acknowledged correct AI and compensated for AI misses.
links.quote: Gastroenterologists who had access to AI support called for AI support in 90% (162/180) of the cases before training, which dropped to 57.8% (104/180) after training ( p < 0.001).

links.outcome: External validation of CNN on out-of-distribution data
links.effect: AI was tested only on a single-centre dataset split by patient; no external dataset testing was possible and performance on out-of-distribution data remains unknown.
links.quote: As we generated a unique in vivo endocytoscopic high-quality BE dataset of 520-fold magnified images, we were unable to test the performance of the CNN with external datasets.

unlisted_practices: Training clinicians in a novel classification system before AI-assisted interpretation

links.effect: Cross-over gastroenterologists with AI had sensitivity +12.89% (2.11–23.67), p = 0.024 versus AI model alone.
links.quote: Additionally, they outperformed the sensitivity of the AI model alone (+12.89% (2.11–23.67), p = 0.024) ( Figure 4 D).

links.effect: AI-assisted follow-up sensitivity 91.11% vs 71.11%; accuracy 82.78% vs 70.56%.
links.quote: AI-assisted gastroenterologists scored substantially better than unassisted gastroenterologists in establishing an optical biopsy of Barrett’s-associated dysplasia through EC.

links.quote: Additionally, they outperformed the sensitivity of the AI model alone (+12.89% (2.11–23.67), p = 0.024) ( Figure 4 D).
